stem: A father asks a Massachusetts community pharmacy to obtain a prescription-labeled naloxone product through the pharmacy's authorized naloxone prescription/standing-order pathway because his adult daughter recently survived an opioid overdose. The daughter is not present. Which conclusion is most defensible?

choices.text: The pharmacy must refuse because naloxone may be supplied only to the person at risk.
The father must first be diagnosed with opioid use disorder before he can receive naloxone.
The request must be processed as an emergency Schedule II opioid prescription.
A lawful Massachusetts naloxone pathway can include a person positioned to assist someone at risk of overdose.
Community pharmacies may provide naloxone only when an emergency department transfers the patient’s prescription.

explanation.core_reasoning: Massachusetts opioid-antagonist access is intentionally broader than direct-to-patient dispensing. A family member positioned to respond to an overdose can fall within the lawful third-party access framework.

choice_analysis.A: The law does not require the naloxone recipient to be the person who is personally at risk.
choice_analysis.B: The assisting person need not have opioid use disorder to qualify as a third-party recipient.
choice_analysis.C: Naloxone access is not governed by treating naloxone as a Schedule II opioid.
choice_analysis.D: This matches the third-party assistance purpose of the Massachusetts naloxone framework.
choice_analysis.E: The statute contemplates pharmacy access and is not limited to emergency-department transfers.

related_facts: Prescription naloxone and FDA-labeled OTC naloxone are separate products under current Massachusetts DCP guidance.
Massachusetts prescription naloxone access can place rescue medication with a third party positioned to assist.
explanation.mpje_trap: The person receiving the naloxone does not have to be the person expected to receive naloxone during an overdose.

reasoning_steps: Identify the requester as a third party positioned to assist
Apply the Massachusetts opioid-antagonist access rule
